```{python}
import polars as pl
import requests
import io
import numpy as np
from lets_plot import *

LetsPlot.setup_html(isolated_frame=True)
```

```{python}
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/byuidatascience/data4missing/master/data-raw/flights_missing/flights_missing.json"
response = requests.get(url)
df = pl.read_json(io.BytesIO(response.content))
```

## QUESTION 1

__Calculate the sample size (i.e. number of rows in the dataset) for each airport in each year.__ What do you notice?

The table below shows the number of rows per airport per year. A few things stand out right away. First, most airport-year combinations have **10–12 rows** — roughly one row per month, which makes sense for monthly data. However, ATL has **23 rows where the year is null**, meaning those records are missing a year value entirely. This is a data quality issue that would need to be addressed before any year-level analysis. Second, some airport-year combos have only 9–11 rows instead of 12, which suggests a month or two of data is missing for those periods. The dataset generally appears structured but has noticeable missingness in the `year` column for ATL.

```{python}
q1 = (
    df
    .group_by(["airport_code", "year"])
    .agg(pl.len().alias("row_count"))
    .sort(["airport_code", "year"])
)

q1
```

## QUESTION 2

__Which airport has the worst delays?__ Describe the metric you chose, and why you chose it to determine the "worst" airport. Your answer should include a summary table that lists (for each airport) the total number of flights, total number of delayed flights, proportion of delayed flights, and average delay time in hours.

**Metric chosen: Proportion of delayed flights**

To determine the "worst" airport for delays, I used the **proportion of flights that are delayed** (total delayed flights ÷ total flights). This metric is the most fair for comparing airports of vastly different sizes — a large hub like ATL handles millions more flights than SAN, so raw delay counts would be misleading. Proportion puts all airports on an equal footing.

A secondary metric worth noting is **average delay time in hours** (total minutes delayed ÷ total delayed flights ÷ 60). An airport could delay fewer flights but make each delay much longer — that matters too.

**Finding:** **SFO (San Francisco)** has the worst delays by proportion, with about **26.1% of all flights delayed** — the highest of any airport in the dataset. It also has the second-highest average delay time at just over 1 hour per delayed flight. ORD (Chicago O'Hare) is a close second at 23.1% and actually has the longest average delay time of any airport (~1.13 hours).

```{python}
airport_summary = (
    df
    .group_by("airport_code")
    .agg([
        pl.col("num_of_flights_total").sum().alias("total_flights"),
        pl.col("num_of_delays_total").sum().alias("total_delayed_flights"),
        (
            pl.col("minutes_delayed_total").sum() / 60.0 /
            pl.col("num_of_delays_total").sum()
        ).alias("avg_delay_hrs"),
    ])
    .with_columns(
        (pl.col("total_delayed_flights") / pl.col("total_flights"))
        .alias("prop_delayed")
    )
    .select([
        "airport_code",
        "total_flights",
        "total_delayed_flights",
        "prop_delayed",
        "avg_delay_hrs",
    ])
    .sort("prop_delayed", descending=True)
)

airport_summary
```

## QUESTION 3

__Create a barplot showing the proportion of all flights that are delayed at each airport. Describe what you learn from this graph.__

The bar chart confirms the ranking from Question 2 visually. **SFO stands clearly apart** — more than 1 in 4 flights at San Francisco International are delayed, the highest proportion among all 7 airports. ORD is second, with nearly 1 in 4 flights delayed. At the other end, **SLC (Salt Lake City)** is the most reliable airport in the dataset, with only ~14.6% of flights experiencing any delay. The gap between SFO and SLC is roughly 11 percentage points — a meaningful difference for travelers trying to pick a low-risk routing.

For the CEO's flight booking app, this suggests SFO and ORD routes should carry a higher delay warning label, while SLC routes can be marketed as more reliable.

```{python}
# Prepare data for plot (sorted best to worst for visual clarity)
plot_data = airport_summary.sort("prop_delayed", descending=True)

(
    ggplot(plot_data, aes(x="airport_code", y="prop_delayed"))
    + geom_bar(
        stat="identity",
        fill="#2E6DA4",
        color="white",
        width=0.65,
    )
    + geom_text(
        aes(label="prop_delayed"),
        format=".1%",
        position=position_nudge(y=0.003),
        size=10,
        color="#333333",
    )
    + scale_x_discrete(
        limits=plot_data["airport_code"].to_list()
    )
    + scale_y_continuous(
        labels=".0%",
        limits=[0, 0.32],
    )
    + labs(
        title="Proportion of Flights Delayed by Airport (2005–2015)",
        subtitle="SFO and ORD have the highest delay rates; SLC is the most reliable",
        x="Airport Code",
        y="Proportion of Flights Delayed",
        caption="Source: Bureau of Transportation Statistics"
    )
    + theme_light()
    + theme(
        plot_title=element_text(size=14, face="bold"),
        plot_subtitle=element_text(size=11, color="#555555"),
        axis_title=element_text(size=11),
        axis_text=element_text(size=10),
    )
)
```
